title: Northbreeze Private VPC Onramp and Region Guardrails Discovery
summary: Intro discovery for Northbreeze's private onramp to Redwood Private. Covered networking topology options (VPC peering, PrivateLink/private endpoints, transit gateway), egress and IP management, region gating (EU-only for PII), KMS/HSM for key control, and pilot scope. Agreed next steps: share network checklist, security whitepaper, test account request, and schedule deep-dive with Tomas and Samir on routing and IP planning.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-04 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 mins | Platform: Zoom (recording enabled)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Ellen (Northbreeze VP Eng), Tomas (NetOps), Priya (Security), Samir (Infra)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for doing this. quick intro from our side, i'm Maya, AE on the enterprise team. Jordan is our SE who will handle the deep network bits.
[00:22] Ellen: Hi all, Ellen here. Our goal today is to understand how Redwood Private would fit into our VPC model and what we need to prepare network and security wise.
[00:35] Jordan: Cool. at a high level we support three deployment modes — hosted, dedicated, and private. Today we'll focus on Private — that's the VPC onramp style where the inference plane sits in your VPC or connects privately.
[01:05] Tomas: Quick clarifying question — when you say "sit in our VPC" do you mean we bring your image into our subnets or you peer into our VPC? we have strict egress controls so we need to know the topology options.
[01:22] Maya: Yeah great point. There are two common patterns: 1) VPC peering/transit gateway where Redwood's service peered with your VPC and we announce routes; or 2) Private endpoints/Privatelink style where you establish a private endpoint in your VPC and traffic goes over AWS backbone to Redwood-managed infra. Jordan, can you add detail?
[01:45] Jordan: Sure. For the peering/transit gateway model we typically ask for a small set of route advertisements and a dedicated transit attachment; that gives low latency but requires you to accept route tables. The private endpoint model does not require route table changes — you create interface endpoints (ENIs) and we terminate there. Tradeoff: peering may be simpler for high-throughput streaming because no extra ENI NAT hop, private endpoints are simpler for strict route isolation.
[02:30] Tomas: We prefer not to accept route advertisements automatically, we prefer explicit IP allow lists and NAT egress. Also we have to keep all PII workloads in EU regions only.
[02:45] Priya: Right — data residency is our hard constraint. Any talk of fallback to hosted must ensure there is no cross-region data leakage. We also need KMS control for model keys and audit logs for each inference request for compliance.
[03:05] Jordan: We support customer-managed KMS — you can bring keys via KMS or HSM integrations. Our control plane has options: customer-managed keys for token encryption and we can push audit logs to your S3 or Splunk via private endpoints. Small note: sometimes the transcription of docs calls says K-M-S as K M S slash H S M which is non helpful, but we do support HSM-backed flows.
[03:30] Ellen: Ok that's good. On egress IPs — we need a stable egress IP set so our firewall rules at our partner network can allow outbound callbacks. how do we present egress IPs in private mode?
[03:47] Jordan: In private mode with private endpoints, the egress remains within your VPC so the external egress comes from your NAT gateways; Redwood doesn't introduce additional public egress IPs. For peering/transit there is normally an egress path from Redwood side for some control plane calls — we can lock those to static IPs and provide an allow list. If you use Dedicated we can also provide reserved public egress IP pools.
[04:20] Samir: So for our compliance we want all control plane traffic to originate from EU-only addresses. Is there a region gating capability?
[04:33] Maya: Yes, we have routing policies — you can pin to EU-only regions and block fallback to non-EU. Our policy engine allows region-only rollouts for model variants; fallback is opt-in. We should capture that in the pilot SLA.
[04:55] Tomas: Another piece — throughput. we expect bursty inference patterns during business hours, 10k RPS spikes for short periods. what's the recommended pattern for autoscaling and handling that in a private topology?
[05:12] Jordan: For heavy burst you want dedicated capacity pools in your VPC or partner region. We support autoscaling groups and on-prem-like pools. Two levers: batching and pre-warming. If you have tight latency SLAs you should also enable warm-standby nodes and a canary fallback to hosted for excess traffic (but that's obviously gated by your compliance requirements).
[05:38] Ellen: We probably cannot fallback to hosted for PII, so we need to size for peak or configure throttles.
[05:45] Priya: Which brings me to logs and retention: we require 7 years access to audit logs for certain requests and immutable storage. Can Redwood stream logs to our S3 with server-side encryption using our KMS?
[06:00] Jordan: Yes — we can push audit logs through a private endpoint to your S3 bucket and use your KMS. There are slight delays in ingestion but it's standard. Also we offer token-level costing in the console but for PII we can disable token metadata retention.
[06:28] Tomas: Networking detail — we use transit gateway and multiple VPCs. do you support cross-account endpoints or do you require a single VPC?
[06:39] Jordan: We support cross-account attachment patterns; in AWS you can create interface endpoints in multiple accounts and map tenancy. For transit gateway we ask for a direct attachment from your transit to Redwood's managed TGW attachment. We've had cases where customers wanted a central NAT in a hub VPC — that works but we need the egress IP mapping.
[07:05] Ellen: Can you give an example diagram?
[07:09] Maya: We'll send a topology slide but quick sketch: customer VPCs -> transit gateway -> interface endpoint to Redwood Private or peer to Redwood VPC; traffic stays on backbone; control plane calls to Redwood management plane can be pinned to EU region IPs or go through your peered route.
[07:35] Priya: Security control question — SSO and RBAC. We use SAML SSO and require SCIM for provisioning, plus audit of who invoked model endpoints.
[07:49] Jordan: Redwood supports SAML and SCIM for user provisioning, and we can emit audit trails for API keys and user-level operations. For inference invocation, you can choose to pass user id metadata — we don't store that by default for PII unless you opt into longer retention.
[08:10] Tomas: Regarding NAT and concurrent connections: if interface endpoints create ENIs, do we hit ENI limits? we have big fleets so that matters.
[08:23] Jordan: Good question — ENI limits can be a constraint at scale. That's why for very high throughput we recommend peering/transit gateway where possible because it avoids per-endpoint ENI scaling issues. For private endpoints we can also shard endpoints across subnets to spread ENIs; we'll document recommended ENI/subnet counts for your scale.
[08:53] Ellen: Any known gotchas when doing KMS integration? last time we had one service that couldn't do key rotation without a downtime window.
[09:02] Jordan: We support key rotation; the recommended pattern is to use key aliases and rotate in the customer KMS without downtime because Redwood uses key aliases at call time. But if you use an external HSM with strict custody policies there might be an extra handshake for key retrieval that adds latency — we'll surface that in the KMS runbook.
[09:25] Samir: How about private data plane certificate pinning or mutual TLS? we need mTLS across our peered links.
[09:35] Jordan: We support mTLS on the private endpoints and can integrate with your certificate authority; that is a standard option for Private deployments and required in some regulated customers. We'll provide the cert exchange steps.
[09:55] Maya: Quick pause — any blockers so far from compliance or network standpoint?
[10:01] Priya: The big ones: EU-only region enforcement, customer-managed KMS/HSM, immutable audit logs to our S3, and no fallback to non-EU hosted services for PII. Also SAML+SCIM integration.
[10:17] Maya: All are supported in principle; we'll capture exact options in a security appendix that Jordan will draft.
[10:27] Tomas: For the pilot, what is the minimal footprint? we want a small POC in staging to validate latency and egress mapping.
[10:37] Jordan: Minimal pilot: one model endpoint, 2-3 GPU-backed nodes, interface endpoint in your staging VPC, audit logs stream to your S3, keys in your EU KMS. That should be enough to validate latencies and observe KV cache behavior. note: sometimes docs call KV cache "K-V cash" which is fine, just an autocorrect.
[11:00] Ellen: On the audit side we need to sample inference payloads (redacted) and ensure they never leave EU. can the pilot enforce field redaction?
[11:12] Jordan: We have pre-processing hooks and sanitizer plugins you can deploy in your VPC to strip PII before it hits the model. For EU-only we will ensure the inference execution happens in EU compute and logs stay in your S3.
[11:28] Samir: What about cost visibility? our finance team wants token-level cost but not payloads.
[11:36] Jordan: We can provide token-level billing and usage traces without storing payloads. Our console exposes per-route and per-model breakdowns; we can also push cost exports to your billing pipeline.
[11:52] Maya: Switching to timeline — Ellen, you mentioned governance timeline?
[11:58] Ellen: We're aiming for a staged pilot in Nov, then expanded pilot in Dec, and production rollout in Q1 if security sign-off and performance are good.
[12:12] Maya: Sounds doable. we'll need the network artifacts quickly.

[12:35] -- mid-call deeper networking Q&A (timestamps approximate) --
[12:35] Tomas: In the transit gateway model do you require BGP? we have an MPLS peer to our colos.
[12:46] Jordan: We don't require BGP for the TGW attachment; we can do static route propagation. For colo/MPLS we'll work with your edge team. If BGP is preferred we support that for dynamic routing.
[13:05] Priya: How do you handle peered VPC route table conflicts?
[13:12] Jordan: We recommend non-overlapping CIDRs; if there are overlaps we use NAT or proxying to avoid leaking routes. We'll show patterns in the checklist.
[13:28] Tomas: Do you support PrivateLink with private DNS names?
[13:33] Jordan: Yes — interface endpoints with private DNS override is supported. Note: private DNS means inside your VPC the Redwood API names resolve to the ENI. That sometimes trips up service discovery but is standard.
[14:00] Ellen: Any examples of customers with strict EU-only guards?
[14:05] Maya: Yes — a fintech in EMEA did full private deploy in eu-west-1 with customer-managed KMS and a non-fallback policy. we can share a redacted case study.

[14:25] -- near end, recap and explicit next steps --
[14:25] Maya: To recap: we heard EU-only enforce, customer KMS, audit log streaming, no fallback for PII, need stable egress IPs or egress through your NAT, and pilot timeline for Nov. Action items: I'll send the checklist + topology diagram. Jordan will prepare a KMS + mTLS runbook. Tomas/Samir will send VPC details. Priya will share compliance matrix.
[14:55] Priya: One more question on encryption at rest for model artifacts — is that in your control plane or can we fully control it?
[15:05] Jordan: Model artifacts for Private can be encrypted with your keys if you request it; otherwise Redwood-managed encryption is used for hosted-only models. We'll include options.
[15:25] Ellen: Last question — latency SLOs? we need 99th percentile under 200ms for our small prompt use-case.
[15:33] Jordan: With local EU region and dedicated nodes it's achievable; raw tail latency depends on sequence length and batching. For the pilot we'll run a benchmark to show p50/p95/p99.
[15:50] Maya: Great. we'll send the slide deck and checklist after the call. thanks everyone.

[51:30] Meeting end.

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-attributions (Speaker 1 for Samir), small recognition errors ("K-V cash" for KV cache), and some punctuation missing — quality medium.

References mentioned: topology diagram (to be sent), Private deployment checklist (to be sent), security whitepaper (link to be shared).

Recap (final):
- Redwood supports both peering/transit and private endpoints; tradeoffs discussed.
- EU-only enforcement and customer-managed KMS supported.
- Pilot scope agreed: staging endpoint, KMS integration, audit logs to S3, baseline latency tests.
- Next steps and owners listed in action items.
